heroIntro: In an era of hyper-connected digital media, viral Facebook posts, unverified online YouTube portals, and bitter commercial rivalries, reputation is both a person's most valuable asset and their most vulnerable target. In Bangladesh, Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs), corporate executives, physicians, politicians, and business owners frequently face orchestrated smear campaigns, character assassination, and fabricated accusations designed to extort money or destroy professional credibility. Bangladeshi jurisprudence provides a dual legal remedy: filing a **Civil Suit for Damages** under the law of torts to recover monetary compensation for reputational harm, or initiating **Criminal Prosecution** under Sections 499 and 500 of the Penal Code 1860 and cyber legislation to jail the offender. This comprehensive guide outlines the evidentiary standards for libel and slander, how to draft and serve a mandatory 15-day Legal Notice, court fees in civil damage claims, criminal complaint procedures in the Magistrate Court, and constitutional free speech defenses.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Overview: Legal Remedies for Defamation in Bangladesh
quickAnswer.text: Defamation in Bangladesh can be addressed through two parallel or independent legal channels: (1) Civil Tort Action: Filing a Money Suit for Damages in the Court of the Joint District Judge claiming monetary compensation (often ranging from lakhs to crores of BDT) for damage to reputation and business losses, subject to a statutory maximum ad valorem court fee cap; and (2) Criminal Action: Filing a direct complaint (C.R. Case) under Section 500 of the Penal Code 1860 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate, punishable with simple imprisonment for up to two (2) years, or fine, or both. For online smear campaigns on social media, provisions under cybercrime legislation and Bangladesh Cyber Tribunal also apply.
highlights: Governing Statutes: The Penal Code 1860 (Sections 499, 500, 501, 502), Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (Civil Suits for Tortious Damages), Court-Fees Act 1870, Cyber Security Act / ICT Act.
Two Branches of Defamation: Libel (defamatory statement in permanent written, printed, or digital form) and Slander (transitory spoken defamatory statements).

Mandatory Pre-Suit Notice: A formal 15-day Legal Notice drafted by a Supreme Court advocate demanding unconditional public apology and monetary compensation must be served before instituting a civil suit.
Jurisdiction for Civil Damages: Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the statement was made or published.
Criminal Penalties: Up to 2 years imprisonment plus judicial fine under Section 500 Penal Code.
Ten Statutory Exceptions: Truth published for the public good, fair comment on public conduct, privileged court filings, and reports of judicial proceedings are protected under Section 499.
International Expats Protection: NRBs defamed while residing in the USA, UK, Canada, or Australia can sue local perpetrators through authenticated Power of Attorney.

sections.title: 1. Legal Definition: Libel vs. Slander Under Bangladeshi Law
sections.content:
In Bangladeshi legal jurisprudence, defamation is both a civil wrong (tort) actionable without proof of special damage in written form, and a criminal offence codified in statute. The law draws a classic common-law distinction:

  • Libel: A defamatory statement expressed in some permanent, visible, or recorded form—such as printed newspaper articles, published books, cartoons, television broadcasts, website blog posts, or digital social media statuses (Facebook posts, tweets, YouTube videos). Libel is actionable per se, meaning the law presumes general damage to reputation without the plaintiff having to prove specific monetary financial loss.
  • Slander: A defamatory imputation conveyed through transitory spoken words, gestures, or audible sounds in a public gathering, business meeting, or press conference. Under civil tort law, slander generally requires establishing that the spoken words caused actual special harm or directly imputed a criminal offence, contagious disease, or professional incompetence.

sections.title: 2. Civil Action for Tortious Damages: The Joint District Judge Forum
sections.content:
When a defamatory campaign inflicts catastrophic commercial loss, cancelled contracts, or severe mental agony, a civil lawsuit for monetary damages is the ultimate judicial remedy. Governed by the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC), the civil mechanism operates as follows:

  • Filing Forum: Civil compensation suits for substantial amounts (exceeding 25 Lakh BDT) must be instituted before the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the area where the defamatory publication occurred or where the defendant resides.
  • Establishing the Tortious Elements: To succeed, the plaintiff's advocate must prove three foundational elements: (1) The words were defamatory; (2) The words explicitly referred to the plaintiff (or were reasonably understood by the public to refer to the plaintiff); and (3) The words were published—communicated to at least one third party other than the plaintiff.
  • Injunction Against Further Defamation: Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC, the plaintiff can simultaneously file an application for a Temporary Injunction restraining the defendant, media house, or online platform from further publishing, broadcasting, or circulating the defamatory material pending trial.

sections.title: 3. Criminal Defamation Under Sections 499 & 500 of the Penal Code
sections.content:
For victims seeking swift punitive justice and criminal records against malicious agitators, the Penal Code 1860 provides criminal remedies:

  • Section 499 (The Definition): 'Whoever, by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said... to defame that person.'
  • Section 500 (Punishment): Mandates that whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two (2) years, or with fine, or with both.
  • Section 501 & 502 (Printers and Publishers): Imposes identical 2-year criminal penalties upon anyone who prints, engraves, or sells defamatory materials knowing them to contain character assassinations.
  • Procedure (C.R. Case): A formal petition of complaint is filed directly before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM). The magistrate examines the complainant on solemn affirmation under Section 200 CrPC and issues summons or an arrest warrant against the accused.

sections.title: 4. Social Media & Online Defamation: Facebook, YouTube & Cyber Tribunals
sections.content:
The explosion of online viral misinformation has made social media the primary battleground for reputation warfare in Bangladesh. Digital defamation involves specialized evidentiary and jurisdictional procedures:

  • Evidentiary Preservation: Merely taking a screenshot is insufficient in court because digital evidence can be fabricated. Evidence must be certified under the Information and Communication Technology Act 2006 and the Evidence Act 1872 (as amended in 2022). It is essential to preserve full URL links, video file downloads, IP header logs, server metadata, and execute a formal Notarial Affidavit of Web Preservation before the perpetrator deletes the post.
  • Cyber Tribunal Jurisdiction: If the online defamation involves fake obscene images, morphed videos, deepfakes, or threats to national security or public order, complaints can be lodged directly before the Divisional Cyber Tribunal or the Police Cyber Support for Women / CID Cyber Crime Investigation Division.
  • Takedown Requests: A formal legal notice can be served upon local representatives or parent entities of Meta, Google/YouTube, or local ISPs to remove defamatory URLs under intermediary liability doctrines.

sections.title: 5. The Ten Statutory Exceptions & Defenses to Defamation
sections.content:
Defamation law in Bangladesh balances personal dignity against the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 39 of the Constitution. Section 499 of the Penal Code contains Ten Statutory Exceptions which operate as complete legal defenses:

  1. Imputation of Truth for Public Good: It is not defamation to state true facts concerning any person if the publication is genuinely for the public welfare.
  2. Public Conduct of Public Servants: Expressing good-faith opinions regarding the official discharge of duties by public servants.
  3. Conduct of Any Person Touching Any Public Question: Good-faith opinions respecting the conduct of individuals participating in public affairs.
  4. Publication of Reports of Court Proceedings: Substantially true and accurate reports of proceedings in courts of justice.
  5. Merits of Case Decided in Court: Fair comments on the conduct of witnesses, parties, or judicial decisions after trial conclusion.
  6. Merits of Public Performance: Good-faith critiques of published books, films, theatrical performances, or architecture submitted to the judgment of the public.
  7. Censure by Person Having Lawful Authority: Good-faith disciplinary censure passed by a parent, schoolmaster, employer, or judge over a subordinate.
  8. Accusation Preferred in Good Faith to Authorized Person: Lodging a complaint of crime to a police officer or magistrate in good faith.
  9. Imputation Made in Good Faith for Protection of Interests: Statements made to protect one's own legal rights or commercial property.
  10. Caution Intended for Good of Person or Public: Conveying private warnings in good faith regarding an individual's financial creditworthiness or character.

sections.title: 6. Drafting the 15-Day Legal Notice: Mandatory Evidentiary Steps
sections.content:
Before rushing into a civil courtroom, delivering a devastating, airtight Legal Notice is an indispensable strategic step:

  • Service via Registered Post with A/D: The notice must be drafted by an enrolled advocate and served upon the perpetrator via Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due (A/D) and courier service, creating an indisputable record of delivery.
  • Core Demands: The notice must set forth: (a) The exact defamatory statements quoted verbatim with date and publication medium; (b) The falsity and malice behind the statements; (c) A strict demand for an unconditional written apology published in the identical prominent medium within fifteen (15) days; and (d) A specified liquidated financial sum demanded as damages for reputational devastation.
  • Evidentiary Role in Trial: If the defendant fails to reply or issues an arrogant, evasive response, that refusal is exhibited in court as prima facie evidence of continuous malice, vastly strengthening the plaintiff's claim for exemplary punitive damages.

sections.content:
Choosing the correct legal path depends on whether your ultimate goal is financial compensation, criminal imprisonment, or instant digital content removal. The table below delineates the statutory options:

sections.title: 8. Court Fees, Quantum of Damages & Valuation Caps
sections.content:
A critical consideration in instituting a civil money suit for defamation is calculating the mandatory ad valorem court fee under the Court-Fees Act 1870:

  • Statutory Maximum Court Fee Cap: Unlike jurisdictions where plaintiffs can claim 100 Crore BDT without paying fees, Bangladeshi law prevents frivolous claims by requiring an ad valorem fee of approximately 2% on the claimed amount. However, the law provides a statutory maximum cap (presently capped at approximately 50,000 to 60,000 BDT depending on statutory amendments) for civil plaints.
  • Assessment of Quantum: In awarding damages, civil courts examine: (1) The social, professional, and commercial standing of the plaintiff; (2) The gravity and venom of the false accusation (e.g., alleging embezzlement, moral turpitude, or treason); (3) The extent of circulation (local gossip vs. nationwide prime-time television broadcast); (4) Provable commercial loss, cancelled deals, or lost contracts; and (5) The subsequent conduct of the defendant.

sections.title: 9. Protecting Non-Resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) Against Smear Campaigns Abroad
sections.content:
Expatriates living in North America, Europe, and the Middle East are favorite targets of blackmail syndicates and predatory relatives in Bangladesh. Rogue elements often circulate fabricated videos, forge false matrimonial complaints, or spread rumors in village communities to force NRBs to forfeit ancestral land or yield to extortionate demands.

Under Bangladeshi procedural law, an NRB defamed while living abroad does not need to abandon their career and travel to Bangladesh to initiate legal action. By executing a Special Power of Attorney attested by the nearest Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission, an overseas citizen can empower a Supreme Court advocate or trusted representative in Dhaka to:

  • Serve legal notices demanding retractions and apologies.
  • Institute a formal Criminal Defamation Complaint (C.R. Case) before the Magistrate Court.
  • File a Civil Money Suit for Damages with an immediate application for a Gag Order / Injunction.
  • File an emergency report with the CID Cyber Crime Division to block overseas access and remove malicious Facebook posts.

sections.title: 10. Real-Life Case Study: Recovering 1-Crore Damages for Business Defamation
sections.content:
The managing director of an ISO-certified pharmaceutical export company in Tejgaon, Dhaka, became the target of a vicious smear campaign orchestrated by a terminated procurement officer. The ex-employee launched multiple anonymous Facebook pages, circulated doctored letters alleging that the company's exported medicines were contaminated, and emailed foreign importers in the UK and Australia.

The company engaged our legal chamber to dismantle the malicious campaign. Our multidisciplinary legal strategy was executed as follows:

  1. Secured forensic digital evidence via a Notarial Certificate of Web Preservation, documenting IP connections, email headers, and timestamps before pages could be wiped.
  2. Issued an emergency 15-day Legal Notice to the perpetrator's permanent address and served formal takedown notifications to Meta Platforms Inc.
  3. Instituted a Criminal Case under Section 500 of the Penal Code before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Dhaka. The Magistrate took cognizance, recorded depositions, and issued an immediate arrest warrant.
  4. Concurrently filed a Civil Suit for Damages (Money Suit No. 19/2023) before the 1st Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, claiming 1 Crore BDT in commercial damages, alongside an application under Order XXXIX CPC.
  5. The Joint District Judge granted an immediate temporary injunction restraining the defendant and his agents from uttering or publishing any statements concerning the plaintiff.
  6. Facing imminent criminal arrest by DB Police and escalating civil liability, the perpetrator surrendered in court, submitted an unconditional judicial apology published in two national dailies, and executed a formal settlement deed paying substantial monetary compensation.

faqs.question: What is the legal difference between libel and slander in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Libel is defamation in permanent or written form (such as newspaper reports, printed letters, books, website posts, or Facebook statuses) and is actionable without proof of actual financial damage. Slander is defamation in temporary, spoken words or gestures and generally requires proving actual harm or severe personal imputations.

faqs.question: What is the maximum criminal punishment for defamation in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Under Section 500 of the Penal Code 1860, criminal defamation is punishable with simple imprisonment for up to two (2) years, or with a judicial fine, or with both.

faqs.question: Is it mandatory to send a Legal Notice before filing a defamation lawsuit?
faqs.answer: While not strictly mandatory for criminal complaints, serving a 15-day Legal Notice through an advocate is practically indispensable before filing a Civil Suit for Damages. It establishes prior notice, proves persistent malice, and affords the defendant an opportunity to issue an apology.

faqs.question: Can I sue someone for defaming me on Facebook or YouTube in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Online defamation can be prosecuted criminally before the Magistrate Court under Section 500 Penal Code or before the Cyber Tribunal under cyber security legislation, as well as pursued for monetary damages in the Civil Court.

faqs.question: What court has jurisdiction over civil defamation suits for money damages?
faqs.answer: Civil suits claiming significant monetary compensation for reputational damages are instituted before the Court of the Joint District Judge having territorial jurisdiction over the place where the defamatory material was published or where the defendant resides.

faqs.question: Is stating the truth considered a complete defense against defamation?
faqs.answer: Under the First Exception to Section 499 of the Penal Code, stating the truth is a complete defense only if it is published for the public good. Simply proving that a statement is factually true may not suffice if it was published purely out of private malice without any public interest.

faqs.question: Can an NRB living in the US or UK sue someone in Bangladesh for defamation?
faqs.answer: Yes. An overseas Bangladeshi can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, authorizing a Supreme Court advocate or representative in Bangladesh to institute civil suits and criminal complaints.

faqs.question: Can a civil court issue a gag order stopping someone from continuing defamatory posts?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a plaintiff can apply for a Temporary Injunction restraining the defendant from publishing or uttering further defamatory material while the suit is pending.
